strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses genuine bottleneck in scaling Boltzmann Generators to realistic systems via principled coarse-graining approach

Sound theoretical framework: Rigorous connections between force matching error and distributional accuracy (Proposition 1 via Log-Sobolev inequalities); clever exploitation of fiber distribution invariance in ESFM

Rigorous experimental methodology: Careful force recomputation for unbiased labels, proper dataset generation with unbiased/biased variants, transparent comparisons using explicit solvent as reference
Practical contributions: Demonstrates PMF learning from short biased trajectories (10 ns), simulation-free evaluation paradigm for CG potentials, improvement over implicit solvent models
Thorough supplementary materials: Detailed algorithms, comprehensive ablations (weight clipping sensitivity), extensive appendix with reproducibility details
weaknesses: Limited experimental scope undermines scalability claims: Only tested on alanine dipeptide (22 atoms), one of smallest systems in contemporary literature; no validation on larger proteins or realistic systems; scalability narrative not empirically justified

Concerning effective sample size: ESS ≈ 0.23 indicates 77% sample rejection; no theoretical analysis of ESS degradation with system dimensionality; modest efficiency raises fundamental questions about applicability to higher-dimensional problems

Weight clipping introduces unquantified systematic bias: 1% truncation discards samples to stabilize estimates; Figure 12 shows bias-variance tradeoff but provides no principled criterion for threshold selection; no evidence that 1% is universal across systems

Insufficient baseline comparisons: No direct comparison with atomistic BGs on identical systems; missing comparisons with recent CG Boltzmann Emulators (Lewis et al. 2025, Zheng et al. 2024) despite extensive citations; no comparison with classical CG force fields

Critical dependence on predefined collective variables: Requires domain expertise; limited study of sensitivity to CV choice; CV discovery relegated to future work despite being essential for generality and practical applicability

Theoretical dependencies weaken self-contained contribution: ESFM Propositions 2-3 attributed to Chen et al. (2026, concurrent work); Proposition 1 assumes global LSI which is strong assumption for multimodal PMFs

Asymmetric computational comparison: All-atom baseline generates solute-only coordinates (authors note full configs would be infeasible); reduces validity of speedup claims; true wall-clock speedup (3x) is modest

strengths: Sound mathematical framework with rigorous propositions connecting force matching error to distributional accuracy, though with appropriate caveats about LSI assumptions.

Comprehensive experimental validation across toy systems and multiple peptide sizes with both biased and unbiased training data, demonstrating convincing recovery of equilibrium distributions after reweighting.
Significant practical advantage: enables training from 10ns of enhanced sampling MD instead of 500+ ns of unbiased MD (50× data efficiency gain), addressing a real bottleneck in prior work.
Excellent presentation quality with clear writing, effective visualizations (Ramachandran plots, free energy profiles), and rigorous documentation of methods, hyperparameters, and results.
Honest discussion of limitations including LSI assumptions, coarse-graining degeneracy, and weight clipping necessity, with thorough ablation studies supporting design choices.
Novel simulation-free PMF evaluation capability enabling rapid assessment of candidate coarse-grained potentials without additional simulations.
weaknesses: Scalability claims not fully validated: largest demonstrated system is 72-atom hexapeptide; true applicability to realistically-sized protein systems (>100 residues) remains undemonstrated.

Approximation bias from learned PMF is mitigated pragmatically (1% weight clipping) rather than principally resolved; the clipping threshold is chosen ad-hoc from sensitivity analysis without fully principled justification.
Incomplete independence from prior work: Propositions 2-3 and ESFM framework are attributed to Chen et al. 2026, reducing conceptual novelty despite solid engineering integration of these components.

Still requires predefined collective variables for coarse-graining, a major practical bottleneck that severely limits applicability to complex systems; recent CV discovery methods are mentioned but not integrated.
Selective biasing of only 1 of N dihedral pairs during MetaD for larger peptides may incompletely sample relevant degrees of freedom; sensitivity to this choice is not thoroughly investigated.

Atomistic BG baselines (TarFlow, ECNF++) are trained on biased implicit solvent data, making direct comparison unfair and limiting assessment of improvement over properly-trained explicit solvent atomistic BGs.

Coarse-graining degeneracy problem (increasing conditional variance with aggressiveness) is identified but not quantified; unclear if or how it can be mitigated for practical use on highly coarse representations.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates the scalability-accuracy trade-off between atomistic BGs and Boltzmann Emulators, and proposes a principled solution
Solid theoretical framework: Propositions 2-3 on ESFM rigorously establish that learned PMFs preserve mean forces under CG biasing, enabling practical learning from rapidly converged data

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple systems (MB potential, dipeptide/tripeptide/hexapeptide), biased/unbiased regimes, multiple CG resolutions, explicit solvent reference, careful force label verification
Demonstrated practical improvements: Successfully recovers equilibrium statistics from biased/short trajectories; outperforms implicit solvent baselines; significant computational speedup (Table 1)
Reproducibility: Detailed algorithms in appendix, complete architectural/hyperparameter specifications, promised code release, single-GPU feasibility
Honest evaluation: Reports results across different settings, includes ablation studies (weight clipping sensitivity), acknowledges limitations and failure modes
Novel secondary contribution: Simulation-free PMF benchmarking (Section 4.3) enabling rapid model validation without MD simulations
weaknesses: Limited scalability demonstration: Systems remain small (≤72 atoms); ESS degrades significantly with size (0.51 for dipeptide → 0.12 for hexapeptide), raising questions about practical applicability to larger systems with no theoretical explanation provided

Approximation bias unresolved: Weight clipping (1%) is essential for stability (Tables 7-9 show severe degradation without it), introducing explicit bias despite 'asymptotically correct' claims; bias-variance trade-off not rigorously analyzed

Limited experimental scope: Only peptides + toy potential tested; all systems have clear dihedral CVs limiting generalizability; missing comparisons to alternative coarse-graining methods and recent Boltzmann Emulator variants

Theoretical gap between assumptions and practice: LSI assumption acknowledged as 'strong' but not verified empirically; PMF approximation error not bounded in terms of network capacity; connection between force matching and distributional accuracy could be more rigorous

Design choices not fully justified: Different biasing schemes for different peptides (only φ,ψ for dipeptide vs. single pairs for tripeptide/hexapeptide); no principled CG resolution selection strategy; no guidance on when method will fail

Presentation clarity: Notation switching (r vs R) requires careful reading; intuition behind force matching → importance sampling connection could be clearer; no analysis of why conditional force variance increases under coarser mappings
Missing negative results and failure analysis: No pathological examples shown; unclear when CG mapping introduces information loss or when predefined CVs are inadequate
